title: Relations, Composition, and Reachability
summary: You will learn to represent binary relations (binäre Relationen) as directed graphs (gerichtete Graphen) and 0/1 matrices. Composition (Komposition) links consecutive steps; powers of a relation (Relationpotenzen) describe paths of a precisely specified length. You will practice distinguishing paths, reachability (Erreichbarkeit), and common pitfalls involving matrices and algebraic laws.
keyFacts: A binary relation E on V is a subset of V×V; an edge x→y corresponds to the pair (x,y)∈E.
The geometric positions of the vertices in a graph drawing do not change the relation.
The less-than-or-equal relation on ℕ₀ can be defined as {(a,a+b) | a,b∈ℕ₀} and contains every loop.
For fixed enumerations of sets A and B, the relation matrix (Relationsmatrix) for R⊆A×B has size |A|×|B|; rows represent starting elements and columns represent destination elements.
With the set enumerations reversed, the matrix of the converse relation (Umkehrrelation) Rᵀ is the transpose of the matrix M_Rᵀ.
In the relational product (relationales Produkt) RS, R is applied first and then S; an intermediate vertex must connect both steps.
Boolean matrix multiplication (boolesche Matrizenmultiplikation) combines entries with AND and aggregates possible intermediate vertices with OR; it does not count paths.
Composition (Komposition) is associative, has identity relations as neutral elements, distributes over union, and is monotone.
The relational product is generally not commutative and does not generally distribute over intersection.
For an endorelation, R⁰=Id_A, and Rᵏ describes paths of exactly k steps.
R^{≤k} is the union of the powers of R from R⁰ through Rᵏ; R^{<k} includes the powers from R⁰ through Rᵏ⁻¹.
A path of length k has k edges and k+1 vertex entries; the relation Rᵏ stores only the starting and ending vertices.
A pair belongs to Rᵏ exactly when there is a path of length exactly k between its elements.
On a finite vertex set A with n vertices, R^{<n}=R^{<k} for every k≥n.
The finite bound (Endlichkeitsschranke) applies to unions of powers; it does not mean that individual powers become equal from some index onward.

review.notes: Matrix-Transponierungsfrage präzisiert; Prüfskript zur Matrixdimension ergänzt. Prüfskripte zur Diagrammfrage in Vertiefen und zum reflexiv-transitiven Abschluss korrigiert. VO8/VO9-Wiederholungsfragen behalten; source.heading ist dort null.

questions.prompt: A binary relation $E$ on a vertex set $V$ is represented as a directed graph. When is there an edge $x\to y$?

options.text: Exactly when $x$ or $y$ is not in $V$.

questions.explanation: The directed edge goes from the first to the second entry of the relation pair. A reverse arrow corresponds to the pair with the entries swapped.

questions.prompt: If the vertices are arranged differently in a graph drawing, the relation represented by the graph changes.
questions.explanation: The directed edges determine the relation. The geometric positions and edge crossings carry no mathematical information.

questions.prompt: For fixed enumerations of the sets $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}$ and $B=\{b_1,\ldots,b_n\}$, the relation matrix satisfies: $r_{i,j}=1$ exactly when ___.
questions.explanation: A 1 marks a pair whose first entry is the element indexing the row and whose second entry is the element indexing the column.

questions.prompt: Which pairs does the converse relation $R^\top$ contain if a pair $(x,y)\in R$ is given?
questions.explanation: The converse relation swaps the entries in every pair. For fixed enumerations, this corresponds to transposing the matrix.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the relation matrix $M_R$ of a relation $R\subseteq A\times B$ are correct? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: The rows represent elements of the source set $A$.
Every relation matrix must be square.
For $|A|=m$ and $|B|=n$, it has $m$ rows and $n$ columns.
A different enumeration order can change the matrix even though $R$ remains the same.

questions.explanation: The dimensions follow from the enumerations of A and B. A matrix is square only if the two sets have the same number of elements.

questions.prompt: Which definition describes the less-than-or-equal relation on $\mathbb{N}_0$?
questions.explanation: Since $b\ge 0$, we have $a\le a+b$. Conversely, every pair $a\le c$ can be written in this form with $b=c-a$.

questions.prompt: Which of the following directed edges is present directly in the graph shown?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  A((A)) --> B((B))
  B --> C((C))
context.caption: The arrows indicate direction and direct edges.

questions.explanation: A directed edge from $u$ to $v$ corresponds to the relation pair $(u,v)$. The edge $A\to B$ is present directly. The path from $A$ through $B$ to $C$ is not a direct edge from $A$ to $C$.

questions.prompt: Suppose the relational product is defined by $(a,d)\in RS$ exactly when there is an $x$ such that $(a,x)\in R$ and $(x,d)\in S$. Complete the sentence: A path described by $RS$ begins with a step from ___.
questions.explanation: By the given definition, the first step goes from $a$ to $x$ via $R$. Only then does the step from $x$ to $d$ via $S$ follow.

questions.prompt: How is an entry computed in Boolean matrix multiplication?

options.text: Compare the matrix entries independently of the intermediate vertex.
For each intermediate vertex, take the AND of the two entries and combine the results with OR.
For each intermediate vertex, add the entries and multiply all the sums.
Add the rows of the two matrices.

questions.explanation: A shared intermediate vertex requires a 1 in both corresponding entries. The result is 1 as soon as at least one such intermediate vertex exists.

questions.prompt: If two different intermediate vertices connect a start and a destination, the corresponding entry of the Boolean product is $2$.
questions.explanation: Boolean multiplication checks only whether at least one intermediate vertex works. Multiple paths still give an entry of 1.

questions.prompt: What is $R^0$ for an endorelation $R$ on $A$?
questions.explanation: The zeroth power describes zero steps. Therefore, every vertex is connected to itself, so $R^0=\mathrm{Id}_A$.

questions.prompt: Given $R=\{(p,q),(r,q),(s,p)\}$ and $S=\{(q,u),(p,v)\}$, determine the relational product $RS$.
questions.explanation: For p and r, the R-step leads to q, and from there S leads to u. For s, R leads to p, and then S leads to v.

questions.prompt: A pair $(u,v)$ belongs to $RS$ if there is a path from $u$ to $v$ that first traverses an edge labeled $R$ and then one labeled $S$. Which of the following pairs belongs to $RS$?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  p((p)) -->|R| q((q))
  q -->|S| s((s))
  q -->|R| t((t))
context.caption: The label on each arrow indicates the corresponding relation.

questions.explanation: The path $p\xrightarrow{R}q\xrightarrow{S}s$ shows that $(p,s)\in RS$. The edge from $q$ to $t$ is labeled $R$, so it cannot serve as the required second step from $S$.

questions.prompt: Compute the transpose of the matrix $M_R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.explanation: Transposing swaps rows and columns. The 2×3 matrix therefore becomes a 3×2 matrix.

questions.prompt: For $R=\{(a,b),(b,c)\}$, $(a,c)\in R^2$, but $(a,c)\notin R$.
questions.explanation: The path $a\to b\to c$ has exactly two edges and shows that the pair belongs to $R^2$. A direct edge from a to c is not in R.

questions.prompt: Compute the Boolean dot product of the row $(1,0,1)$ and the column $(0,1,1)^\top$. Combine with AND and aggregate with OR.
questions.explanation: The three AND results are 0, 0, and 1. Their OR is 1; the matches are not added to get 2 or 3.

questions.prompt: A relation has a source set $A$ with 2 elements and a target set $B$ with 3 elements. What are the dimensions of its relation matrix?
questions.explanation: The rows correspond to A and the columns to B. The matrix therefore has 2 rows and 3 columns.

questions.prompt: Which statements about relational composition hold in general? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: Identity relations act as neutral relations.
Composition distributes over union on both sides.

questions.explanation: Associativity, the identity property, and both distributive laws over union hold. However, the order of the steps can matter, so composition is not generally commutative.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{x,y\}$, let $R=\{(x,y)\}$. Determine $R^{<1}$.
questions.explanation: $R^{<1}$ is the union of $R^0$ through $R^0$ and is therefore just the identity relation on A. The edge from R is not included.

questions.prompt: What form does a path of length 2 have?

options.text: Two vertex entries and one edge; in $R^2$, the path is stored in full.
Two vertex entries and two edges; in $R^2$, the intermediate vertex is also stored.
Three vertex entries and three edges.
Three vertex entries and two edges; in $R^2$, only the start–destination pair is recorded.

questions.explanation: Path length counts edges, so a path of length 2 contains three vertex entries. The relation pair contains only the start and end.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{p,q,r\}$, let $R=\{(p,q),(q,q),(q,r)\}$. Determine $R^2$.
questions.explanation: From p, the path goes via q to q or r. From q, it goes via q to q or r. r has no outgoing step.

questions.prompt: For every endorelation $R$, $R^2=\mathrm{Id}_A$ holds because two steps must return to the starting vertex.
questions.explanation: $R^2$ contains all start–destination pairs connected through an intermediate vertex by exactly two R-steps. Returning to the start is not required.

questions.prompt: Which statements about composition distributing over intersection are correct? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: Composition always distributes over intersection exactly as it does over union.
On the left-hand side, the same S-edge must belong to $S_1$ and $S_2$.
The equality $R(S_1\cap S_2)=(RS_1)\cap(RS_2)$ does not hold in general.
On the right-hand side, two different intermediate vertices may be used.

questions.explanation: For the left-hand side, a shared S-edge must exist. On the right-hand side, two different intermediate vertices may connect the same start and destination, so the two sides can differ.
$S_1$ and $S_2$ have no edge in common, so the left-hand side is empty. On the right, both products yield the pair $(0,3)$, but via different intermediate vertices.

questions.prompt: Does $(u,w)$ belong to $R^2$? An entry belongs to $R^2$ exactly when there is a path with exactly two R-edges.

context.content:
flowchart LR
  u((u)) --> v((v))
  v --> w((w))
  u --> x((x))
  x --> z((z))
context.caption: Directed graph R

options.text: No, because there is only one path with two edges.
No, because $u$ has no outgoing edge.

questions.explanation: The path $u\to v\to w$ uses exactly two edges. Therefore, the start–destination pair $(u,w)$ belongs to $R^2$.

questions.prompt: A pair in $R^k$ describes reachability in at most $k$ steps.
questions.explanation: $R^k$ represents exactly k steps. Reachability in at most k steps is captured by the union $R^0\cup R^1\cup\cdots\cup R^k$.

questions.prompt: For an endorelation on a finite set with $n$ vertices, the following holds for every $k\ge n$: $R^{<k}=___$.
questions.explanation: With n vertices, every reachable pair can be connected by a path with fewer than n edges. The lemma concerns the union of the powers.

questions.prompt: What does $(a,b)\in R^2$ mean?

options.text: There are exactly two distinct paths from $a$ to $b$.
The relation contains the same edge $(a,b)$ twice.
There is an intermediate vertex $x$ such that $aRx$ and $xRb$; the two edges need not be identical.
There is a path from $a$ to $b$ with at most two edges.

questions.explanation: The second power connects two consecutive R-steps through an intermediate vertex. It counts neither repeated edges nor the number of possible paths.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{a,b,c\}$, let $R=\{(a,b)\}$. Determine $R^{\le1}$.
questions.explanation: $R^{\le1}=R^0\cup R^1$. Add the identity pairs for all three vertices and the one edge from R.

questions.prompt: Relational composition is commutative because it is associative.
questions.explanation: Associativity only allows parentheses to be regrouped. It does not allow the order of the relations to be swapped; in general, $RS\ne SR$ may hold.

questions.prompt: Which statements explain why composition is associative? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: Associativity follows from composition being commutative.
A pair belongs to both sides exactly when suitable intermediate vertices $b,c$ connect the steps $aRb$, $bSc$, and $cTd$.
With either grouping, the steps are performed first with $R$, then with $S$, and then with $T$.
The order of the relations stays the same; only the grouping changes.

questions.explanation: Both sides describe the same sequence of three steps and the same existence conditions for intermediate vertices. No swapping of the relations is needed.

questions.prompt: Suppose $R_1\subseteq R_2$ and $S_1\subseteq S_2$. Which inclusion follows from the monotonicity of composition?
questions.explanation: Every intermediate vertex that works for the smaller pair of relations also works in the respective larger relations. Thus, every pair in the product remains included.
The intersection $S_1\cap S_2$ is empty. In the two products on the right, however, the same start–destination pair can arise via two different intermediate vertices.

questions.prompt: Which of the following relations contains the pair $(1,4)$? We are looking for the power with exactly three steps.
questions.explanation: The path $1\to3\to2\to4$ has exactly three edges. Thus, $(1,4)$ belongs to $R^3$, but not to $R$ or $R^2$.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{p,q,r,s\}$, let $R=\{(p,q),(q,r),(q,s),(s,p)\}$. Determine $R^2$.
questions.explanation: From p, the path goes via q to r or s; from q, it goes via s to p; from s, it goes via p to q. r has no outgoing step.

questions.prompt: For an endorelation $R$ on $A$, let $R^0=\mathrm{Id}_A$, $R^{<1}=\bigcup_{i=0}^{0}R^i$, and $R^{\le1}=\bigcup_{i=0}^{1}R^i$. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.
questions.explanation: The union bounds show that $R^{<1}$ contains only R⁰, while $R^{\le1}$ includes R⁰ and R¹. R⁰ is the identity, and R¹ is R.

questions.prompt: For a graph with $n$ vertices, every reachable pair has a path with fewer than $n$ edges; however, this does not imply $R^n=R^{n-1}$ in general.
questions.explanation: A reachable pair can be connected by a path with no repeated vertices and at most n−1 edges. The lemma compares unions of powers, not individual powers.

questions.prompt: A relation $R$ on $A=\{a,b,c\}$ contains exactly the pairs $(a,b)$ and $(b,c)$. Here, transitivity means that $xRy$ and $yRz$ must imply $xRz$. Which assessment is correct?

options.text: $R$ is transitive because $(a,c)$ automatically belongs to $R^2$.
$R$ is not transitive because $(a,c)$ is missing.
$R$ is neither transitive nor a relation.
$R$ is transitive because its two existing pairs are different.

questions.explanation: From $aRb$ and $bRc$, the stated condition also requires $aRc$. This pair is missing from R.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\{x,y\}$ and $R=\{(x,y)\}$. Define $R^+=\bigcup_{k\ge1}R^k$ as the set of all pairs connected by a path of positive length, and let $R^*=\mathrm{Id}_A\cup R^+$. Determine $R^*$.
questions.explanation: One step goes from $x$ to $y$, so $R^+$ contains the pair $(x,y)$. No further steps are possible. The identity relation on $A$ adds $(x,x)$ and $(y,y)$.

questions.prompt: In Boolean matrix multiplication, a row and a column are compared across possible intermediate vertices. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: Two suitable intermediate vertices make the result entry equal to two.
A suitable intermediate vertex requires a 1 in both corresponding entries.
A product entry is 1 if at least one intermediate vertex works.
The operation represents existence, not the number of paths.

questions.explanation: AND checks a single intermediate vertex, and OR aggregates all possibilities. Thus, the operation records whether a path exists, not how many paths there are.

questions.prompt: What does $R^{\le2}$ mean for an endorelation $R$?

options.text: Reachability in fewer than 2 steps, but with no zero-step paths.

questions.explanation: $R^{\le2}=R^0\cup R^1\cup R^2$. The index ≤ allows all path lengths from zero through two.

questions.prompt: If, for a finite set $A$ with $n$ elements, the equality $R^{<n}=R^{<k}$ holds for every $k\ge n$, then the individual powers $R^n$ and $R^{n-1}$ must also be equal.
questions.explanation: The finite bound concerns the cumulative unions $R^{<n}$ and $R^{<k}$. It does not make any claim about equality of individual powers.

questions.prompt: For relations, suppose that $(a,d)\in XY$ exactly when there is an $x$ such that $(a,x)\in X$ and $(x,d)\in Y$; thus in $XY$, an $X$-step comes first, followed by a $Y$-step. Given $R=\{(0,1)\}$ and $S=\{(1,2)\}$, determine $RS$ and $SR$.
questions.explanation: For $RS$, the $R$-step goes from $0$ to $1$, then the $S$-step goes from $1$ to $2$. For $SR$, the first step would have to be from $S$ and then continue with an $R$-step; however, there is no outgoing $R$-edge from $2$.

levels.title: Applications: Paths, Networks, and Surprising Numbers

questions.prompt: You are planning a route with exactly two travel segments. The destination of the first segment must be the starting point of the second. Which idea describes the possible start–destination pairs?

options.text: Less-than-or-equal relation: sort locations by name
Relational product: connect two consecutive steps through a shared intermediate location
Identity relation: stay at every location
Converse relation: swap the start and destination of every segment

questions.explanation: When planning the route, the two segments must connect at the same intermediate location. This is the idea of the relational product: it links one step to the next.

questions.prompt: In a social network, $F$ means “follows.” A follows B, and B follows C. Here, $F^2$ describes pairs connected by exactly two consecutive follow edges. Is the following statement true: $(A,C)$ then belongs to $F^2$, but this does not prove that A follows C directly?
questions.explanation: The two follow edges form a path from A through B to C, so $(A,C)$ belongs to $F^2$. Therefore, the pair need not already belong to the direct follow relation $F$.

questions.prompt: You are creating a 0/1 relation matrix for 4 source systems and 7 destination systems. How many cells does the matrix have?
questions.explanation: Each row corresponds to a source system and each column to a destination system. The matrix therefore has $4\cdot7=28$ cells.

questions.prompt: In a database, you link employees to teams and teams to offices. A report should return “Yes” for each employee–office pair if at least one shared team lies between them—even if several teams match. Which concept fits this set-theoretic model?

options.text: Ordinary matrix multiplication: matching intermediate values are returned as a count
Converse relation: read all assignments in the opposite direction
Relational product: a shared intermediate entry connects two assignments
Relation power $R^3$: exactly three assignments must follow

questions.explanation: The team is the shared intermediate point between an employee and an office. The relational product asks whether at least one such intermediate point exists; multiple matches still yield “Yes.”

questions.prompt: A small traffic network has vertices P, Q, R, and S, and directed edges P→Q, P→R, Q→S, R→S, and S→P. $R^2$ contains pairs connected by exactly two edges; identical start–destination pairs are counted only once. How many distinct pairs does $R^2$ contain?
questions.explanation: For each possible intermediate destination, check whether one edge leads there and another edge then leads to the final destination. The resulting pairs are (P,S), (Q,P), (R,P), (S,Q), and (S,R): 5 in total. The two different paths from P to S still give only one pair.

questions.prompt: In a game, each portal transition takes you from one zone to another; this step relation is $R$. $R^3$ means that three such transitions are carried out in succession. Which pairs does $R^3$ describe?

options.text: Zones connected by exactly three portal transitions
Zones connected by at most three portal transitions
Zones with a direct portal transition between them
The number of all possible portal routes

questions.explanation: A power of a relation $R^k$ describes paths with exactly $k$ steps. Thus, $R^3$ consists of starting and destination zones connected by exactly three portal transitions.

questions.prompt: A directed dependency network has 8 packages. If one package is reachable from another, repeated packages can be removed from a suitable dependency chain. How many arrows can such a chain have at most?
questions.explanation: After removing repetitions, the path has at most 8 distinct vertices. Between 8 vertices there can be at most 7 consecutive edges, so the chain has 7 arrows.

questions.prompt: An admin dashboard displays a 0/1 matrix: rows are requesting servers, columns are reachable destination servers, and a 1 indicates a direct permitted connection. You want to represent the same connections in the opposite direction. What do you do?

options.text: Square the matrix: combine two consecutive connections
Transpose the matrix: swap rows and columns
Keep only the diagonal: connections from a server to itself
Add the entries: count multiple paths

questions.explanation: The converse relation swaps the start and destination in every pair. In the matrix representation, this corresponds to transposing the matrix, which swaps its rows and columns.

questions.prompt: A network has 3 devices. A relation on it may contain or omit any ordered pair of devices; loops such as device A→device A are allowed. How many different relations are possible?
questions.explanation: There are $3\cdot3=9$ possible ordered pairs. Each can independently be included or omitted, so there are $2^9=512$ different relations.

questions.prompt: A package manager checks whether package A indirectly depends on another package Z. An arrow $X\to Y$ means: package X directly depends on package Y. A chain of such direct dependencies may lie between A and Z. What is the package manager looking for?

options.text: Only a direct dependency between A and Z
A path with exactly two dependency steps
The geometric positions of package names in a drawing
Reachability via a path of arbitrary length

questions.explanation: An indirect dependency means that a path from A to Z exists. In a finite network, any reachable pair can also be connected by a path with no repeated vertices.
